title: Louisville Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Louisville wells have a 150 ft median depth, 10 gpm median yield, and typical finished costs of $13,500-$22,500.
h1: What Louisville, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Well records within 5 miles of Louisville show a wide range of conditions. The median permitted well is 150 feet deep, with the middle half between 30 and 300 feet. Reported yields have a 10.0 gallons-per-minute median, but only 507 wells report a pump yield, so nearby records are useful evidence rather than a guarantee.

Most permits are tied to Denver Basin aquifers or unnamed fractured-bedrock conditions. That makes the exact lot, formation, and neighboring well history important. If you are buying in Louisville, Paragon Estates, Superior, Lafayette, or toward Broomfield, review the actual permits around the property before relying on a seller's description.

sections.heading: Louisville well depth depends on the formation
sections.html:
Louisville-area well depths vary substantially. The median is 150 feet, while the middle half runs from 30 to 300 feet. Forty-three percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet, 30% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 22% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 6% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 1,989 feet.

For a drilling bid, do not treat 150 feet as a promised target. It is a planning midpoint. A lot with nearby shallow wells may still require a deeper hole if the water-bearing interval is different. The records identify 3,217 wells in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, 203 in Laramie Fox Hills, and 154 in alluvial aquifers. Those conditions can change over short distances.

sections.heading: What Louisville wells produce
sections.html:
Among wells with reported pump yields, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 8.0 to 15.0 gpm. The distribution is fairly favorable on paper: 64% report 5 to 15 gpm, 28% report more than 15 gpm, 6% report 1 to 5 gpm, and 2% report under 1 gpm.

That low-yield share matters to a buyer. A well producing under 1 gpm may still serve a home with storage, but it gives less margin for household use, irrigation, leaks, or future construction. Only 507 wells in the records report a pump yield, so ask for the well test, pump information, and actual production history rather than assuming the neighborhood median applies to the property.

sections.heading: Louisville water levels and the record over time
sections.html:
The median static water level is 19 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 8 to 42 feet. That is a relatively shallow measured water level compared with the range of drilling depths, but static level is not the same as sustainable well production. It can also vary with season, pumping, and measurement method.

The decade series does not show a simple continuing decline. Median measured depth to water was 27 feet in the 1950s, 37 in the 1960s, 20 in the 1970s, 70 in the 1980s, 23 in the 2010s, and 10 in the 2020s. Only 143 wells report static water levels, so the 1980s increase should not be treated as proof of a basin-wide trend. Check the specific well and nearby measurements.

sections.heading: Permit history points to long local drilling experience
sections.html:
There are 4,093 Colorado DWR permit records in the Louisville search area, with 2,379 recorded as constructed. Permits span several decades, and the newest permit year is 2025. The largest permit totals by decade are 652 in the 1990s, 463 in the 1970s, 368 in the 2010s, and 355 in the 2000s.

The most active drillers in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 676 wells; Waneka & Son Drilling (Waneka, Don), with 487; and Ground Water Systems Inc (Wilson, Richard R.), with 238. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation or a current bid. Confirm licensing, availability, scope, and recent references before hiring.

sections.heading: Louisville drilling cost starts with depth
sections.html:
For Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, the local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 150-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $7,500 to $10,500. That is only the hole, not the complete water system.

A finished well including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $13,500 to $22,500 at the median depth. A deeper-than-median hole can move the bid higher, and the final price depends on casing, grout, access, formation conditions, and the equipment needed. Get a written scope that separates drilling from pump installation, electrical, trenching, testing, and permit-related work.

sections.heading: Louisville lots need environmental and septic review
sections.html:
Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 427 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 116 historic mine features, and 30 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped locations do not establish contamination at a particular parcel, but they are a reason to test the well and check the property's position relative to known sites. Ask for recent water-quality results and the well construction record.

Low yield, dry holes, and fractured-bedrock variability are practical risks. Septic setbacks, drainfield space, access for a rig, and the location of the house can affect the usable building area. A DWR permit is not a water-quality certificate. Confirm the permitted use, household needs, septic design, and any augmentation-plan requirements that apply to the basin before closing or building.

sections.heading: Before buying or building near Louisville
sections.html:
Start with the closest constructed wells, not just the neighborhood average. Compare their depths, aquifers, reported yields, static levels, use, and construction details. A cluster of similar records near a parcel gives a driller better information for a bid, while a sharp change in depth or formation is a warning to investigate further.

For an existing home, obtain the well permit, pump test, water-quality tests, treatment history, and repair records. For vacant land, have a Colorado well contractor evaluate rig access and likely siting before you finalize the house plan. Domestic or household use accounts for 56% of the records, while monitoring wells account for 23%, so do not mistake every mapped well for a residential supply. Build the well, septic, access, and electrical plan together.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Louisville, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well within 5 miles of Louisville is 150 feet deep. The middle half ranges from 30 to 300 feet. Forty-three percent are under 100 feet, while 22% are between 300 and 600 feet. Local depth varies because permits involve unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, Laramie Fox Hills, and alluvial conditions.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Louisville?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 150-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $7,500 to $10,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $13,500 to $22,500. A deeper hole or difficult access can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Louisville wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 10.0 gpm median, with the middle half from 8.0 to 15.0 gpm. Sixty-four percent report 5 to 15 gpm, while 2% report under 1 gpm. Only 507 wells report a yield, so request the specific well's test and production records before relying on area statistics.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Louisville, Colorado?
faq.a: The permit records do not prove that a well is safe to drink. There are 427 PFAS sampling or contamination sites mapped within about 10 miles, along with 30 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property's water for relevant contaminants, review treatment history, and compare results with the well's construction and location.

faq.q: Are Louisville well water levels going down?
faq.a: The available decade data does not show a simple continuing decline. Median measured depth to water was 27 feet in the 1950s, 70 feet in the 1980s, 23 feet in the 2010s, and 10 feet in the 2020s. However, only 143 wells report static levels, so check measurements from the specific property and nearby wells.
